cover.title: The narrowbody race and the 787: what Boeing should do differently
cover.subtitle: Debrief of the 2030-2050 war game (four decision rounds: 2030, 2035, 2045, 2050) for the CEO, the CFO and the head of Commercial Airplanes

slides.action_title: Boeing kept its balance sheet safe, but came three years late to narrowbodies and left $2.2B on the widebody

stats.label: Value Boeing created (present value at 2026). Airbus created +$23.37B
Boeing narrowbody share in 2040, below the 40% line. It recovers to 47% from 2049
Objectives met: balance sheet and engine supply met, both narrowbody-share goals missed
Value a 2030 787 Re-engine would have added, with widebody share at 74.8% by 2050

bullets: Airbus's new narrowbody (NGSA) entered service in 2037 and ours (the fps) in 2040. Those three years alone put Airbus at 63% in 2039.
The fps works. From 2040 it more than doubles Boeing's operating profit, and our share climbs back to 47%.
The balance sheet was never at risk. Net debt reached zero in 2029 and stayed there through the fps cash peak, even in the stress case.
Our answer: keep the fps plan, add the 787 Re-engine in 2030, protect the 2040 date and both engine sources, and reset the narrowbody goal.
slides.takeaway: Our answer is the same fps and the same safe balance sheet, plus the 787 Re-engine in 2030, for more than four times the value.
slides.source: War game dash-2050-obj: the game master's final valuation, market shares and objective scoring. Value on the dashboard basis (new-airplane business, present value at 2026).
slides.notes:
WHAT TO SAY: Three findings. (1) We lost the narrowbody race on the calendar. Both companies launched in 2030, Airbus with a 7-year plan and Boeing with a 10-year plan, so Airbus had the market to itself from 2037 to 2040. (2) Our airplane and our balance sheet both did their job: the fps more than doubles profit, and net debt stayed at zero. (3) The widebody, where we lead, was left untouched. A 787 Re-engine launched in 2030 was worth more than everything else we did. Slide 7 has four moves. Only one of them changes what Boeing actually ordered.

SOURCES: +$0.66B (Boeing) and +$23.37B (Airbus) are the game master's final value created against the status quo, as present value at 2026 on the dashboard basis (fact pack: pv_bridge and dpv_all). 38% in 2040 and 47% from 2049 are Boeing's narrowbody delivery shares (nb_share). 63% in 2039 is Airbus's peak (nb_share). 5 of 7 is the game master's objective scoring (boeing_objectives): met were the three balance-sheet lines and the two engine-supply lines; missed were the 50/50 split and the 40% incumbency line. +$2.20B is the replayed plan 'fps 10-year + 787 Re-engine' (+2.86) minus the plan played (+0.66), both from plans_2030, computed with python. It equals Boeing's 2030 regret in the game master's table. 74.8% is Boeing's widebody share in 2050 with a 2030 787 Re-engine (re787_by_round). 'More than four times' is 2.86 / 0.66 = 4.3, computed with python. EIS dates 2037 and 2040 come from the fact pack's timeline. Net debt at zero in 2029 comes from the game master's balance-sheet tracker (net_debt, boeing_objectives). The profit doubling comes from boeing_profit ($6.67B to $14.32B in 2040).

slides.action_title: Airbus's new narrowbody flew three years before the fps: Boeing fell to 37% before the fps took it to 47%

annotations.text: NGSA enters service: Airbus pulls ahead

bullets: Today Airbus delivers 60% of narrowbodies and Boeing 40%.
Both launched in 2030. NGSA entered service in 2037 and the fps in 2040. Airbus peaked at 63% in 2039.
Boeing was below its 40% line from 2037 to 2041. The fps then added about a point a year, reaching 47% from 2049.
The first to market collects first. Airbus's operating profit doubled in 2037, from $8.82B to $18.26B a year. Ours moved only in 2040.
slides.takeaway: We lost the narrowbody race on the calendar, not on the airplane.
slides.source: War game dash-2050-obj: the game master's narrowbody delivery shares by year, programme timeline and dashboard operating profit (2026 prices).
slides.notes:
WHAT TO SAY: This is the state of the narrowbody game. Airbus starts with 60% of the market. Both companies launched a new airplane in the same year, 2030. Airbus chose a 7-year path and was in service in 2037. We chose a 10-year path for schedule headroom and to protect the balance sheet in a downturn, so we arrived in 2040. For three years Airbus had the only new airplane. Our share slid to 37% in 2039 and was 38% in the 2040 test year, so we missed the 40% incumbency line. Once the fps flew, it won back about one point a year, to 47% for good. Airbus ends at 53%, so its own 60% goal is gone too. The new market is close to an even split, but we got there late.

SOURCES: Shares are from the fact pack's nb_share: Boeing 40% in 2026-2036, then 39 / 38 / 37 / 38 / 39 / 40% in 2037-2042, 43% in 2045 and 47% from 2049; Airbus 60% in 2026, 63% in 2039 and 53% from 2049. The 'below 40% from 2037 to 2041' years were read off nb_share with python. Launch years and service dates are from the fact pack's timeline: NGSA launched 2030, in service 2037; fps on the 10-year ramp launched 2030, in service 2040. Airbus operating profit of $8.82B in 2026-2036 and $18.26B in 2037 is from airbus_profit (dashboard, 2026 prices); 18.26 / 8.82 = 2.07, computed with python. Boeing's profit jump in 2040 is from boeing_profit.

slides.action_title: The fps more than doubles Boeing's operating profit from 2040, but its cost leaves just $0.66B of value today
bullets: Operating profit is $6.67B a year today, $14.32B in 2040 and $16.86B from 2049 (2026 prices).
That extra narrowbody profit is worth $20.30B today. The fps bill ($60.32B) costs $14.91B and its financing $4.73B.
Without the fps our value would be -$3.64B and our share 20% by 2050. Launching it was right: it is worth $4.30B.
In the same game Airbus created $23.37B.
slides.takeaway: The fps is the right airplane, but with a 2040 entry into service it only just pays for itself in today's money.
slides.source: War game dash-2050-obj: the game master's final valuation on the dashboard basis (Boeing's new-airplane business at 2026 prices; value as present value at 2026), and replayed 2030 plans.
slides.notes:
WHAT TO SAY: These are our financial results on the dashboard's basis, which covers the new-airplane business at 2026 prices, with value as present value at 2026. Profit more than doubles once the fps is in service. But the airplane arrives late, so the profit comes late, and in today's money it barely covers the bill and its financing. Net value is +$0.66B. The dashboard calls this figure delta-PV: value created against the status quo. Do Nothing was worse. Without the fps we would have lost $3.64B of value and fallen to 20% of the narrowbody market. So the launch was right. The issue is timing and what we did alongside it.

SOURCES: The bridge is the fact pack's pv_bridge: narrowbody profit against the status quo +20.30, the fps bill (-14.91; the $60.32B bill is charged in 2040 and discounted), the debt penalty (-4.73; the dashboard's financing charge for the debt the programme adds), and value created +0.66. Discounting is at Boeing's 10.5% WACC (brief_r1_boeing.md). Operating profit of $6.67B, $14.32B (2040) and $16.86B (2049 on) is from boeing_profit. 14.32 / 6.67 = 2.15 and 16.86 / 6.67 = 2.53, computed with python. -$3.64B and 20% in 2050 are the replay of 'fps: hold + 787: hold' (Do Nothing) in plans_2030. $4.30B = 0.66 - (-3.64), computed with python; it matches Boeing's 2030 grid (launch value +4.30 in the column that happened). Airbus +$23.37B is from dpv_all. This bridge is the dashboard's P&L and value. The next slide uses the game master's whole-company balance-sheet tracker, a different basis.

slides.action_title: The balance sheet was not the constraint: net debt hit zero in 2029 and stayed there through the fps cash peak

annotations.text: fps cash peak $8.44B; stress-case cash flow still +$2.52B
fps in service: free cash flow $19.83B

bullets: Net debt fell from $22.53B (end-2026) to zero in 2029, from consensus cash flow alone. In the stress case it reached zero in 2030.
The fps spent $3.02B in 2030, peaking at $8.44B in 2036. Free cash flow stayed positive every year, at least $2.52B in the stress case.
From 2027 to 2050 the fps returns $325.7B to owners, $44.0B more than Do Nothing. It pays back against Do Nothing in 2046.
All three balance-sheet goals and both engine-supply goals were met. Both narrowbody-share goals were missed.
slides.takeaway: The 10-year fps left room in the balance sheet for a second, smaller development.
slides.source: War game dash-2050-obj: the game master's balance-sheet tracker (whole company, 2026 dollars, analysts' consensus free cash flow; stress case one-third lower) and objective scoring.
slides.notes:
WHAT TO SAY: This is the CFO's slide, on a different basis from the last one: the game master's whole-company balance-sheet tracker, in 2026 dollars, built on the analysts' consensus. The analysts' cash flow repairs the balance sheet by 2029 before any new programme. The real question was whether a launch would undo that. It did not. The fps cash peak of $8.44B in 2036 still left positive free cash flow in the stress case, where cash flow is one-third below consensus. Once the fps is in service, free cash flow roughly doubles. The point for the next slide: we had headroom, and we did not use it.

slides.action_title: The 787 Re-engine was the biggest unused lever: +$2.2B and 16 points of widebody share if launched in 2030
bullets: We lead widebodies with 58.8% of deliveries, but we held the 787 all game. Our share stayed flat to 2060.
Launched with the fps in 2030, the Re-engine adds $2.20B net, and every balance-sheet line still holds (stress-case cash flow low $2.69B).
It fits our own one-development rule. On the 10-year fps the two programmes overlap only in 2033-35, which is 2 years, our cap.
Airbus's possible answer is an A350 Re-engine, which would cost us $3.58B against holding. Airbus held the A350 in all four rounds.
slides.takeaway: The prize was largest in 2030 and shrank with every round we waited.
slides.source: War game dash-2050-obj: game master replays of Boeing's orders with the 787 Re-engine launched in each round, everyone else's orders as played; Boeing's 2030 payoff grid; Boeing's 2030 ExCo test memos.
slides.notes:
WHAT TO SAY: This is where we left money on the table. We lead the widebody market, and a 787 Re-engine launched alongside the fps would have lifted our widebody share from 58.8% to 74.8% by 2050 and added $2.2B of value, the single largest gain open to us. It did not break the balance sheet. It fitted our own rule of at most two years of overlapping development. Why did we hold it? In 2030 the CEO expected Airbus to launch both NGSA and an A350 Re-engine. If Airbus re-engines the A350, our Re-engine loses $3.58B against holding, and that broke the Board's $1B downside limit. Airbus never did it. Each round we waited, the prize shrank: +$0.65B in 2035, +$0.30B in 2045, almost nothing in 2050.

SOURCES: The table is the fact pack's re787_by_round. Each row replays Boeing's actual orders with the 787 Re-engine launched in that round, with every other company's orders as played. Gains are each launch value minus +0.66, computed with python. Widebody share 58.8% is from wb_share. The $2.20B net breaks down as +$5.58B widebody profit, -$2.04B extra bill, -$1.04B extra financing and -$0.31B two-front strain. These are the differences between the bridges of 'fps 10-yr + 787 Re-engine' and the plan played in boeing_fin.json (alts), computed with python. Lowest stress free cash flow is $2.69B in 2034 (plans_2030); the stress-case debt line is met. The 2033-35 overlap (2 years, inside Boeing's 2-year cap, $1.2B strain undiscounted) is from Boeing's 2030 CEO and CFO records (exco_result_r1.json). The $3.58B comes from Boeing's 2030 grid (boeing_grid_2030): with an A350 Re-engine the plan scores -2.70 against +0.88 for holding the 787, or -5.54 against -1.96 if NGSA also launches. Airbus's A350 holds are in the orders for all four rounds (fact pack, orders). The CEO's expected case (NGSA plus an A350 Re-engine) is from Boeing's own 2030 decision record. The Board's -$1B downside limit is from Boeing's 2030 Board guidance.

slides.action_title: Only a faster fps lifts narrowbody share, and it costs value or the stress-case balance sheet; the 787 does not
bullets: A 7-year fps enters service with NGSA in 2037. It gives 44% in 2040, 49% in 2045 and 50% in 2050, which meets the 40% line.
But its bill is bigger ($65.00B against $60.32B) and its cash peaks at $12.54B in 2034, so stress-case cash flow turns negative.
Only the 737 rate increase holds the balance sheet: 6 of 7 goals, but $2.48B less value than our pick, above the Board's $2B cap.
No plan open in 2030 reaches 50% in 2040, so the 50/50 goal was out of reach.
slides.takeaway: Buy value with the 787. Do not buy back 2040 share with a schedule bet.
slides.source: War game dash-2050-obj: game master replays of Boeing's 2030 plans with everyone else's orders as played; Boeing's 2030 Board guidance ($2B cap on value given up for objectives).
slides.notes:
WHAT TO SAY: This is the trade-off you face. Speed is the only lever that moves narrowbody share. A 7-year fps arrives with NGSA, holds the 40% line and gets within a point of parity by 2045. But it is a bigger bill packed into fewer years. With the 787 Re-engine on top, it breaks the stress-case balance sheet and our own two-year overlap rule. Paired with a 737 rate increase instead, it holds the balance sheet and meets 6 of 7 goals. That costs $2.48B of value against our pick, more than the $2B the Board lets us give up for objectives in a round. And it bets on hitting 2037 to the year: the 787-8 was planned for May 2008 and delivered in September 2011. Our view: take the value on the widebody, and keep the narrowbody on the date we can trust. These are replays with everyone else's orders as played, and Airbus might have answered a faster fps differently.

SOURCES: Every row is the fact pack's plans_2030 (value, narrowbody share in 2040 and 2050, stress-case debt line, objectives met). The 49% in 2045 for the 7-year plans is from boeing_fin.json (alts). The 7-year bill of $65.00B, the $12.54B peak in 2034, stress free cash flow of -$0.71B (2034) and stress net debt of $0.47B at end-2035 (7-year alone) are from plans_2030 and the report's net-debt section. The 7-year + 787 Re-engine shows stress net debt of $1.74B at end-2035 and stress free cash flow of -$2.0B (2034). Its overlap is 5 years against Boeing's 2-year cap (Boeing 2030 Board guidance and CFO memo, exco_result_r1.json). The 7-year + 737 rate increase plan dips to -$0.41B stress free cash flow in 2034, but net debt is back to zero by the end-2035 checkpoint, so the line is met (plans_2030). $2.48B = 2.86 - 0.38, computed with python. The $2B cap is Boeing's Board rule on total doctrine plus objective premium (2030 Board guidance). The 787-8 dates are from Boeing's 2030 CFO memo (exco_result_r1.json).

slides.action_title: Keep the fps on its 10-year plan, add the 787 Re-engine in 2030, protect the 2040 date and reset the share goal

recs.recommendation: Launch the fps in 2030 on the 10-year plan, open to all three engine makers.
recs.why: It is the only fps plan that keeps the balance sheet repaired in the stress case, and open engines met both supply goals at no cost.
recs.proof: fps worth +$4.30B against no fps; narrowbody share 47% against 20% in 2050; stress-case cash flow never below $2.52B.

recs.recommendation: Launch the 787 Re-engine in 2030, together with the fps, and announce it first.
recs.why: It is the biggest value lever, it grows the widebody market we already lead, and moving first makes an A350 answer a poor deal for Airbus.
recs.proof: Value +$0.66B to +$2.86B; widebody share 58.8% to 74.8% by 2050; every balance-sheet line held.

recs.recommendation: Protect the 2040 fps date: engines and key suppliers ready by 2036, and the Joint Venture engine proven before entry into service.
recs.why: Every year late leaves NGSA alone in the market, and a covert Airbus Delay Tactics campaign is the main threat to the date.
recs.proof: Three years alone took us to 37%; in the risk case our value falls from +$2.86B to +$1.42B.

recs.recommendation: Reset the narrowbody goal to 47% by 2050, and plan for a dip below 40% in 2037-2041.
recs.why: Our view: no plan open in 2030 reaches 50/50, and buying back the 40% line costs more than it is worth.
recs.proof: Best case 44% in 2040; the 6-of-7 plan gives up $2.48B against our pick, above the Board's $2B cap.

bullets: All four moves keep net debt at zero in both the base and the stress case.
Together they lift value from +$0.66B to +$2.86B and widebody share to 74.8% by 2050. Narrowbody share stays at 38% in 2040 and 47% by 2050.
slides.takeaway: One change to what Boeing did, the 787 Re-engine in 2030, carries the whole $2.2B gain.
slides.source: War game dash-2050-obj: game master replays of Boeing's 2030 plans and of the 787 Re-engine by round; Boeing's 2030 payoff grid; objective scoring; Boeing's 2030 and 2035 Board guidance.
slides.notes:
WHAT TO SAY: Four moves. Move 1 is what we did, and we should keep it. The 10-year plan is the one that keeps the balance sheet safe in a downturn, and opening the fps to all three engine makers met both supply goals for free. Move 2 is the change: launch the 787 Re-engine in 2030, alongside the fps, and say so first. It is worth $2.2B and 16 points of widebody share. Move 3 is execution. Our narrowbody problem was the calendar, so the date is sacred: engines and suppliers ready by 2036, and the Joint Venture engine proven before 2040. Move 4 is candour about the goal. 50/50 from 2040 was never reachable, and chasing the 40% line costs more than it is worth. Set 47% by 2050 as the goal and manage the 2037-2041 dip with customers.

SOURCES: Rec 1: +$4.30B = 0.66 - (-3.64) (plans_2030, python). 47% against 20% in 2050 is from plans_2030 (played and Do Nothing). $2.52B is the stress-case free cash flow low in 2036 (boeing_cash). The 10-year is the only fps ramp that holds the stress line without a rate increase (plans_2030). Engine supply met at code 'all three makers' with zero payoff effect (boeing_objectives; Boeing's 2030 brief says engine choice does not change Boeing's value). Rec 2: values from plans_2030 and re787_by_round, widebody share from re787_by_round, debt lines from plans_2030. 'Moving first' rests on the game master's 2030 stage-game analysis (fact pack, stage_equilibria): one equilibrium pairs Boeing 'fps 10-year + 787 Re-engine' with Airbus 'NGSA + A350 hold + Delay Tactics (one move)', so Airbus's best reply to our Re-engine is to hold the A350. Rec 3: 37% (2039) is from nb_share. +$1.42B is the 2030 grid's risk case, NGSA plus covert Delay Tactics, for 'fps 10-yr + 787 Re-engine' (boeing_grid_2030). The difference of $1.44B was computed with python. Boeing's 2035 Board estimated that covert Delay Tactics cost the fps 5 points of share for 5 years from entry into service (exco_result_r2.json). Rec 4: 44% in 2040 and 49% in 2045 are the best 2030 plans (plans_2030; boeing_fin.json alts). $2.48B = 2.86 - 0.38 (python). The $2B cap is from Boeing's 2030 Board guidance. Bullet 2: value and share from plans_2030 and re787_by_round.

slides.action_title: The main risk is an Airbus A350 answer to the 787 Re-engine; the move is worth it unless the odds pass 4 in 10

risks.risk: Airbus answers our 787 Re-engine with an A350 Re-engine
risks.trigger: Airbus announces an A350 Re-engine in the same round as ours
risks.cost: $3.58B against holding the 787 (value -5.54 against -1.96 if NGSA also launches). Break-even at a 38% chance of an answer
risks.mitigation: Commit first and in public in 2030. The game's model makes holding the A350 Airbus's best reply, and Airbus held it in all four rounds

risks.risk: Two developments at once stretch engineering and cash
risks.trigger: fps stage-gate KPIs slip during the 2033-35 overlap, or cash flow falls more than a third below consensus
risks.cost: Programme cash $66.52B against $60.32B; strain of $0.31B already counted; stress-case cash flow low $2.69B in 2034
risks.mitigation: Separate 787 and fps teams, KPI-gated stage gates, no buybacks before the 2036 cash peak

risks.risk: The fps slips, or Airbus slows it covertly with Delay Tactics
risks.trigger: A missed fps stage gate, or engine or supplier shortages before 2040
risks.cost: Value +$2.86B falls to +$1.42B; Board estimate: 5 points of narrowbody share for 5 years
risks.mitigation: Fund lagging suppliers, engines first. Reset once and conservatively, never cancel

risks.risk: The Joint Venture engine stumbles and the fps is back on CFM alone
risks.trigger: A durability finding on the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine
risks.cost: Engine-supply goal lost. CFM/GE, down to 27% of narrowbody engines from 76%, must carry the whole fleet
risks.mitigation: Durability gate before 2040, CFM kept qualified at full rate, door open to a third source

bullets: All alternatives are replays: what if Boeing had ordered differently, with everyone else as played. A real Airbus might answer differently.
The dashboard is a stylised model of the market. It shows how incentives interact; it is not a forecast.
slides.takeaway: Move first on the 787, guard the fps date, and keep a second engine source alive.
slides.source: War game dash-2050-obj: Boeing's 2030 payoff grid; the game master's 2030 stage-game analysis; replayed 2030 plans; narrowbody engine shares; Boeing's 2035 Board guidance and 2045 public statement.
slides.notes:
WHAT TO SAY: Be straight about the risks. The big one is Airbus answering the 787 Re-engine with an A350 Re-engine. If it does so in the same round, our Re-engine costs $3.58B against holding. If it does not, our Re-engine earns $2.2B. So the move pays as long as the chance of an Airbus answer is below about 4 in 10. The game's model says Airbus's best reply to a Boeing Re-engine is to hold, the widebody works like a game of chicken where the first to commit wins, and Airbus held the A350 in every round. Our view: an answer that comes later would cost less than the same-round figure. The second risk is doing two developments at once. The overlap is two years, inside our rule, and its strain is already in the numbers. The third is a late fps, whether our own slip or Airbus slowing our suppliers. The fourth is engines: the Joint Venture made our two engine sources depend on one new engine.

SOURCES: $3.58B is from boeing_grid_2030: 787 Re-engine against hold is -2.70 against +0.88 (A350 Re-engine only) and -5.54 against -1.96 (NGSA plus A350 Re-engine), computed with python. Break-even = 2.20 / (2.20 + 3.58) = 0.38, computed with python. It uses the same-round grid, where the gain is +2.20 in the columns with no A350 answer. The stage equilibrium comes from the fact pack's stage_equilibria for 2030: Boeing 'fps 10-yr + 787 Re-engine' with Airbus 'NGSA + A350: hold + Delay Tactics (one move)', at +1.42 / +24.08. Airbus's A350 holds are in the fact pack's orders. Risk 2: programme cash $66.52B against $60.32B and strain -$0.31B are from boeing_fin.json alts; the $2.69B low in 2034 is from plans_2030; the 2033-35 overlap is from Boeing's 2030 memos. Risk 3: +$1.42B is the 2030 grid's risk case for our pick (boeing_grid_2030). 5 points for 5 years is from Boeing's 2035 Board guidance (exco_result_r2.json). Risk 4: Boeing's 2045 public statement, 'If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone' (bulletin_r4.md). CFM/GE's narrowbody engine share of 76% (2026) and 27% (from 2040) is from nb_engine_share.

reviews.verdict: Most numbers check out against the fact pack, boeing_fin.json, grids_r1.json, stage_r1.json, exco_result_r1/r2.json and bulletin_r4.md. That covers the shares, the bridge, the cash tracker, plans_2030, re787_by_round, 3.58, the 38% break-even, 66.52 / 65.00 / 60.32, and the 2033-35 two-year overlap. Both line charts use datasets, series and years that exist. Neither forbidden word (Milk, Sabotage) appears anywhere. Three real errors need fixing before the deck ships. (1) Rec 1 says the 10-year plan is the only fps plan that holds the stress-case balance sheet, but slide 6's own table shows the 7-year + 737 rate increase plan as Held. (2) Slide 5 says the 787 Re-engine 'fits our own one-development rule', but the CEO's one-development-at-a-time rule was one of his reasons for holding it; the 2-year overlap cap is a separate rule. (3) Slide 5's 2045 and 2050 gains should be +0.29 and +0.04, not +0.30 and +0.05: the exact values are 0.2933 and 0.0425, and the game master's regret table gives 0.29 and 0.04. Several should-fix wording and framing gaps are listed below. The main ones: the Delay Tactics mechanics are misdescribed, the 4-in-10 break-even is rounded the wrong way, cash to owners is credited to the fps, and the equilibrium cited for 'moving first' gives +1.42, not +2.86.

issues.problem: Rec 1 'why' says the 10-year fps is 'the only fps plan that keeps the balance sheet repaired in the stress case'. This is false and contradicts slide 6.
issues.evidence: plans_2030: 'fps 7-yr + 737 rate up + 787: hold ... stress debt line met (stress net debt end-2035 $0.0B) ... 6 of 7'. Slide 6 shows that row as 'Held'. The two via-Embraer + 737 rate up plans also meet the line. The notes' own source line is narrower and correct: 'the only fps ramp that holds the stress line without a rate increase'.
issues.fix: 'It is the only fps plan that keeps the balance sheet repaired in the stress case without a 737 rate increase, and open engines met both supply goals at no cost.'

issues.problem: Bullet 3 says 'It fits our own one-development rule.' Boeing's records say the opposite. The one-development-at-a-time rule [BX-1239] was one of the CEO's four grounds for holding the 787 Re-engine. The 2-year overlap cap is a different rule (H4).
issues.evidence: exco_result_r1.json Boeing final rationale: 'I still HOLD the Re-engine on four grounds: the Board's -$1B Downside limit...; my one-development-at-a-time rule [BX-1239]; company doctrine (... no Re-engine before 2036); the premium'. Ops memo: 'It is H4-legal (2033-35, 2 years, $1.2B strain), but it is a second major development at once, against the one-at-a-time doctrine.' Board: 'One development at a time. No 787 Re-engine this round.'
issues.fix: 'It stays inside our 2-year overlap cap: on the 10-year fps the two programmes overlap only in 2033-35. It does mean two developments at once, which our one-at-a-time rule avoids.' In the notes, list all of the CEO's grounds for holding it, not only the -$1B limit.

issues.fix: Print +0.29 (2045) and +0.04 (2050) in the table, the notes and numbers_used. The 2030 and 2035 values, +2.20 and +0.65, are correct.

reviews.verdict: The story is the right shape and most of it reads in plain English. The order is market, results, balance sheet, unused lever, trade-off, recommendations, then risks. Nearly every number traces to the fact pack. But I would not take this into the room tomorrow. Four things would break in front of the CFO and the Board. (1) The "why" for recommendation 1 is contradicted by the deck's own slide 6. (2) The core recommendation, the 787 Re-engine in 2030, is one the Board explicitly said it would veto. The deck says it "fits our own rule" and uses Board limits only where they help the argument. (3) The A350 risk is reassured with "Airbus held it in all four rounds". Yet in hindsight an A350 Re-engine was Airbus's best move in every round, and our own 2030 expected case assumed Airbus would launch it. (4) Slide 3 charges $4.73B of "financing" and slide 4 then says net debt was zero throughout, with no reconciliation on either slide. Beyond those, the cover title states a diagnosis rather than the answer. Several terms are never explained: stress case, Delay Tactics, risk case, Joint Venture engine, strain, and ΔPV in the HTML chart. The case against a faster fps leads with the weaker reason (the balance sheet) instead of the real one (schedule risk).

issues.problem: The 'why' for recommendation 1 is wrong. It says the 10-year plan is 'the only fps plan that keeps the balance sheet repaired in the stress case'. Slide 6's own table shows another fps plan that holds it.
issues.evidence: Slide 6 row 'fps 7-year + 737 rate increase … Stress-case balance sheet: Held, 6 of 7'. In the fact pack, plans_2030 'fps 7-yr + 737 rate up + 787: hold' reads 'stress debt line met (stress net debt end-2035 $0.0B)', and the 10-yr + 737 rate-up rows are met too. The speaker notes hedge it ('only fps ramp that holds the stress line without a rate increase'), but the slide text does not.
issues.fix: Reword the 'why' to: 'It is the only plan that keeps the balance sheet safe in a downturn without also raising the 737 rate, and it leaves room for the 787 Re-engine.' Or simply: 'It is the date we can trust, with 3 years of slack against our usual slip, and it keeps the balance sheet safe.'

issues.problem: The core recommendation, launch the 787 Re-engine in 2030, is exactly what Boeing's Board said it would veto. The deck never says so, and it applies Board rules selectively. It rejects the 6-of-7 plan on the Board's $2B cap, but measures that cap against a plan the Board would itself veto, and it is silent on the Board's -$1B downside limit, which this recommendation breaks by $2.58B. A CEO will ask: 'Are you asking me to overrule my Board, or to change its rule?'
issues.evidence: exco_result_r1.json, Boeing board_guidance. Priorities/3: 'One development at a time. No 787 Re-engine this round: its value falls below -$1B whenever Airbus re-engines the A350'. would_veto/1: 're787: launch … fails Downside in S3 and S4 … -3.58 with the 10-year ramp'. The $2.48B 'given up' on slide 6 and rec 4 is measured against +2.86, the vetoed plan. Measured against the best plan the Board would accept (+0.66 as played), the 6-of-7 plan gives up only $0.28B.
issues.fix: Add one plain line to rec 2: 'This needs the Board to lift its $1B downside limit for this one decision, because the expected gain ($2.2B) beats the downside if the chance of an Airbus answer stays under 4 in 10.' On slide 6 and rec 4, either measure the $2B cap against a Board-acceptable plan, or drop the cap argument and reject the 6-of-7 plan on schedule and value grounds instead.

issues.problem: 'It fits our own one-development rule' is a factual misstatement. The rule it does meet is a different one: the cap of at most 2 years of overlap between developments (H4). The Board's one-development rule rules this move out. Also, '2033-35, which is 2 years' reads as three years to anyone counting.
issues.evidence: Board priority 3 reads 'One development at a time. No 787 Re-engine this round.' The CEO's frame says the Re-engine 'is still governed by H3's second half, by H4 and by my one-development-at-a-time rule'. H4 is the 2-year overlap cap. Fact pack, other facts: the 10-year fps has no development overlap on its own.
issues.fix: Replace it with: 'It breaks our one-development-at-a-time rule, but stays inside our cap of 2 years of overlap (the two programmes run side by side from 2033 to 2035).' Then point to slide 7, where the Board waiver is asked for.

issues.problem: The main risk is understated, and its mitigation rests on false comfort. 'Airbus held it in all four rounds' never tested a Boeing Re-engine. In hindsight, an A350 Re-engine was Airbus's best move in every round. Boeing's own 2030 expected case was that Airbus would launch one, which puts the odds above the deck's 4-in-10 break-even. The slide also leaves out the cost of doing nothing if Airbus moves first.
issues.evidence: Fact pack, regret_airbus: round 1 best 'NGSA + A350 Re-engine + Delay Tactics', regret 3.3; rounds 2-4 best also include 'A350 Re-engine'. Notes on slide 5 say 'In 2030 the CEO expected Airbus to launch both NGSA and an A350 Re-engine' (CEO initial_lean: 'Expected column: … S4'). stage_equilibria 2030 has two outcomes: if Airbus commits first, Boeing gets -3.40 and Airbus +26.67; if Boeing commits first, Boeing gets +1.42 and Airbus +24.08.
issues.fix: Say it straight on the slide. 'Airbus left $3.3B on the table by not re-engining the A350. A smarter Airbus will try. This is a race: whoever commits first wins. If we commit first, Airbus's best reply is to hold. If Airbus commits first, we must hold and we drop to about -$3.4B.' Then make the mitigation dated: 'announce the 787 Re-engine publicly before Airbus's 2030 decision'. Replace 'held in all four rounds' with this logic.

issues.problem: The finance basis contradicts itself across two consecutive slides. Slide 3 charges '$4.73B of financing' (labelled 'Debt penalty' on the chart). Slide 4 then says net debt was zero throughout. The CFO will ask 'what debt?', and neither slide answers. That undercuts the request to underpin the recommendations with Boeing's financial results.

Add one line on slide 3: 'This is the model's charge for tying up cash; in the real balance sheet (next slide) net debt never rises.' reviews.verdict: The storyline mostly holds up. Its core logic matches the fact pack: Boeing lost the narrowbody race on the calendar, the fps launch was right (+$4.30B against Do Nothing), the balance sheet had room to spare, and a 2030 787 Re-engine was the largest unused lever (+$2.20B, and the same +$2.20B over holding in both the S2 and S5 columns). Nearly every number reconciles with factpack.md, boeing_fin.json and the 2030 ExCo record. Four errors must be fixed before the deck goes to executives. (1) The deck says the Re-engine "fits our own one-development rule". In fact it breaks three of Boeing's own 2030 rules: the one-development-at-a-time rule, the -$1B downside limit and the doctrine of no Re-engine before 2036. (2) Rec 1 says the 10-year fps is "the only fps plan" that keeps the stress-case balance sheet, but slide 6 shows another plan that also holds it. (3) "Announce it first" is not possible in the game: in 2030 all orders are sealed and submitted at the same time. (4) The main risk is understated. I replayed the game with the game master's engine, and a later A350 answer costs Boeing more than holding, not less: $4.0-4.8B, so the break-even chance of an answer is about 1 in 3, not 38%. Several should-fix items cover the trade-off framing, the cost of Boeing's own slip, the Delay Tactics case and risks the model does not price.

issues.problem: The deck says the 787 Re-engine 'fits our own one-development rule'. That is false. Launched in 2030, it breaks three of Boeing's own 2030 rules, and Rec 2 never says the CEO and Board must lift them.
issues.evidence: exco_result_r1.json, Boeing board_guidance: 'One development at a time. No 787 Re-engine this round: its value falls below -$1B whenever Airbus re-engines the A350'. Risk appetite: 'no second development'. CEO decision: held the Re-engine on four grounds, namely the Board's -$1B Downside limit, 'my one-development-at-a-time rule [BX-1239]', company doctrine ('no Re-engine before 2036') and the zero premium in his expected column (S4). Only H4, the 2-year overlap cap for 2033-35, is met.
issues.fix: Slide 5: replace the bullet with 'It stays within our 2-year overlap cap (2033-35). But it needs the Board to lift three 2030 rules: one development at a time, the -$1B downside limit (worst case -$5.54B) and no Re-engine before 2036.' Put the same line under Rec 2's 'why' on slide 7 and give the reason for lifting them: a +$2.20B gain over holding, with the balance sheet held in all five 2030 columns.

issues.problem: Rec 1 says the 10-year fps 'is the only fps plan that keeps the balance sheet repaired in the stress case'. Slide 6 contradicts this.

issues.problem: 'Announce it first' (Rec 2) and 'commit first and in public in 2030' (slide 8, risk 1) cannot be done within the game's 2030 levers. Airbus cannot see a 2030 Re-engine before it submits its own 2030 orders, so a same-round A350 answer, the $3.58B case, cannot be deterred. In the 2030 stage game, Airbus prefers the equilibrium in which it re-engines.
issues.evidence: rules.md: 'In each round all five players submit sealed orders at the same time.' Public statements are published in the bulletin after the round. stage_equilibria[1] has two pure equilibria: Boeing hold with Airbus NGSA + A350 Re-engine + Delay Tactics (Airbus +26.67), and Boeing Re-engine with Airbus A350 hold + Delay Tactics (Airbus +24.08). Airbus gains $2.59B in the first.
issues.fix: Replace 'announce it first' with 'launch in 2030; Airbus sees it in the 2035 bulletin, when answering no longer pays for Airbus' (see the next issue for the number). Say plainly that the same-round answer cannot be deterred, only priced. Its cost is $3.58B against holding.

issues.problem: Risk 1 prices only a same-round A350 answer. The notes claim 'an answer that comes later would cost less than the same-round figure', but the model says the opposite. The 16-point widebody gain and the +$2.86B both assume Airbus never re-engines the A350 through 2050, and the deck does not say so. 'Airbus held it in all four rounds' is offered as comfort, but the game master scored those holds as Airbus errors.
issues.evidence: My replays use the method in make_factpack.replay_alt: Boeing's 2030 orders with re787 launched, everyone else as played, Airbus rea350 changed in one later round. Airbus answers in 2035: Boeing -4.83 against -0.80 if Boeing held, which is $4.03B worse; Boeing's widebody share stops at 63.8% from 2040, not 74.8%. Answer in 2045: -4.27 against +0.34 ($4.61B). Answer in 2050: -4.22 against +0.57 ($4.79B). Break-even: 2.20/(2.20+4.03) = 35%, down to 31%. In every case answering also costs Airbus: 22.51 to 21.22 in 2035, 21.80 in 2045, 21.82 in 2050. The game master's regret_airbus names the A350 Re-engine as Airbus's best move in 2035, 2045 and 2050 against Boeing's actual orders.

Replace 'Airbus held it in all four rounds' with the model's reason: an answer after our launch costs Airbus $0.7-1.3B. Label 74.8% and +$2.86B 'if Airbus never re-engines'. Add both replays to the fact pack before use. Name as a model limit that the board values any A350 answer, even one entering service in 2055, as wiping out the Re-engine's value.

issues.problem: The headline +$2.86B assumes Airbus also skips Delay Tactics, yet the 2030 equilibrium the deck cites as proof that Airbus will hold the A350 includes Delay Tactics, and there Boeing gets +$1.42B. Rec 3 treats the drop from +$2.86B to +$1.42B as what protecting the date secures. In the model, though, Delay Tactics take a fixed 5 points of share for 5 years from entry into service, which no Boeing lever prevents, and they do not move the date. final_check.verdict: The numbers are sound, but there is one provenance blocker and several should-fix claims. I checked every number against factpack.md/json, boeing_fin.json, brief_r1_boeing.md, exco_result_r1/r2.json, bulletin_r4.md, rules.md and the game report, using python. The rest checks out: shares (40/37/38/47, 63, 58.8, 74.8), value (+0.66, +2.86, +2.1973, +4.30, -3.64, the 23.37 bridge 20.30/-14.91/-4.73), profit (6.67, 14.32, 16.86, Airbus 8.82 to 18.26), cash and debt (22.53, 2029/2030, 8.44, 2.52, 2.69, 3.38, 19.83, 325.7/281.7/44.0, 136.6, payback 2046), plan rows (1.12, 2.39, 0.38, 0.47/1.74, 5 of 7 / 6 of 7 / 4 of 7), grid (3.58, 1.42, -0.78, -1.44), the 10.5% WACC, $5B/$1.2B, $4.68B, the 787-8 dates, the $10B revolvers, the 2033-35 and 5-year overlaps, the CEO's four reasons, and the 73% engine share. I re-ran the engine myself. It reproduces the debrief-only later-answer replays exactly: 2035 -4.8256 vs -0.7976; 2045 -4.2722 vs +0.3353; 2050 -4.2212 vs +0.5664; Airbus 21.22/21.80/21.82; 63.82% widebody from 2040; break-even 35/32/31%. It also confirms Delay Tactics gives 33% in 2040 and +1.42 / -0.78. Remaining errors: (1) the replay numbers are not yet in the fact pack; (2) "leaves no room for the 787" contradicts Boeing's own 2030 Board guidance; (3) "needs 2037 to the year" overstates what the 40% line needs; (4) the slide-1 notes compare the 787 Re-engine against the wrong baseline; (5) the speaker notes the executives see contain machine names (re787_by_round and other dataset ids); plus a few small wording points.

issues.problem: Unsupported numbers: the later-answer figures are not in the fact pack or any source it names. These are $4.0-4.8B (4.03/4.61/4.79), break-even 35/32/31% ('about 1 in 3'), 63.8% widebody share, and Airbus $0.7-1.3B (21.22/21.80/21.82). The evidence rules require every number to come from there, and the storyline's own numbers_used says 'NOT in factpack.md: add before the deck ships'.
issues.evidence: factpack.md has no row for an Airbus A350 Re-engine answering in 2035/2045/2050. I re-ran the engine (Boeing re787 launch in 2030, Airbus rea350 launch added in round 2/3/4, everyone else as played). Boeing -4.8256 vs -0.7976 (2035), -4.2722 vs +0.3353 (2045), -4.2212 vs +0.5664 (2050). Airbus 21.2244 / 21.7989 / 21.8213. Boeing widebody share 63.82% from 2040 (2035 answer). So the values are right; only the provenance is missing.
issues.fix: Add a 'later Airbus answer' dataset to make_factpack.py and factpack.md/json with these replay results, then cite it. Do not ship slide 8's cost cell, title basis or notes until it is there.

issues.problem: Factual overstatement in the action title, repeated in slide 7 Rec 4's 'why': a 7-year fps 'leaves no room for the 787'. Boeing's own 2030 Board guidance says a 7-year fps leaves room for a Re-engine launched in 2035 within the 2-year cap. Only a 2030 Re-engine is ruled out (5-year overlap).
issues.evidence: exco_result_r1.json, Boeing board_guidance.recommendations[2]: 'A 7-year fps (development 2030-2037) leaves room for a Re-engine launched in 2035 with only a 2-year overlap. A 10-year fps (development 2033-2040) does not.'
issues.fix: Say 'leaves no room for the 787 in 2030' (title and Rec 4 why). The slide 6 notes already scope it correctly ('launched together').

issues.problem: 'It needs 2037 to the year' (bullet 2; also the takeaway and the notes) reads as a condition for holding the 40% line, which bullet 1 just claimed. Under the game's share rule, a 1-2 year slip still holds 40% in the 2040 test year. Only the 44% / 50% parity figures need 2037 exactly. The record's 3-year slip (to 2040, 38%) is what loses the line.
issues.evidence: rules.md, 'How the board sets market shares': the first EIS gains 1 pp a year while alone; from the second EIS shares move 1 pp a year toward 50/50 shifted 1 pp per year of lead. In the game the move applies in the EIS year itself (2039 37% to 2040 38%). So an fps in 2038 gives 39, 40, 41, 42% in 2037-40, and an fps in 2039 gives 39, 38, 39, 40%: both meet 'NB share >= 40% in 2040, 2045, 2050'.
issues.fix: Reword: 'Parity needs 2037 to the year; our clean-sheet record is a three-year slip (787-8), which would put it in 2040 at 38%, below the 40% line.'

issues.problem: The speaker notes say 'A 787 Re-engine launched in 2030 was worth more than everything else we did.' Against what? The fps launch was worth +$4.30B against Do Nothing (slide 3 notes, slide 7 Rec 1 proof), so +$2.2B is not more than it. The claim only holds against the net +$0.66B value created, which is a different baseline (status quo).
issues.evidence: plans_2030: fps 10-yr + 787 hold +0.66 vs fps hold + 787 hold -3.64, so the launch is worth +4.30. The 787 Re-engine gain is 2.86 - 0.66 = 2.1973. The storyline itself uses +$4.30B in Rec 1.
issues.fix: Replace with 'A 787 Re-engine launched in 2030 would have added $2.2B, more than three times the $0.66B of value we created as played.'

Other machine ids also appear (pv_bridge, dpv_all, plans_2030, nb_share, boeing_grid_2030, stage_equilibria, regret_airbus, tracker_inputs, boeing_fin.json, exco_result_r1.json).
